Routes import @midday/supabase/server; the wrapper lives at packages/supabase/src/... specifierPointsAt matches specifier tails against file paths, which handles @/lib/store but not workspace package names.

title: Declared-modules convention materialises as block but its finding reports enforcement_result none
attempted: Reproduced the injection by hand twice (one declared module, then both) - both returned enforcement_result=block. Compared mode vs enforcement across all 7 repos.
evidence: midday is the ONLY repo where enforcement_mode(block) != injection_enforcement(none), and the only one using the --data-modules path. formbricks/calcom/openstatus all use inferred candidates and correctly report block. Finding status is 'new', diff_status 'new_in_diff', engine_source 'rust', so it is not a baseline or fallback artifact. Consequence: blocking_count 0, check_status pass, exit 0 - the guardrail does not fail where the contract says it should.
diagnosis: Isolated to declaredDataModulesCandidate (A6), not the engine: enforcementResultFor and enforcement_mode_from_str both map block correctly, and every inferred-candidate repo matches. Not reproducible by hand, which suggests something about the harness sequence (it injects a clean control route alongside the bad one, and runs a separate F4 probe first) interacts with the declared path.
needs: A focused investigation with the declared path instrumented at the point the engine payload is built. This is an F3-class silent failure - a block-mode contract that returns pass - so it should block beta. enforcement_matches_mode is now recorded per repo in the harness baseline; promote it to a hard assertion once fixed.
reverted_to: n/a - diagnostic field added, no behaviour change reverted

title: Add negative controls to the harness
note: Three per repo: type-only import of the data module (A3/F5), a <dataModule>-legacy lookalike (B3), and a genuine subpath that must still be caught (B3 in the other direction, guarding against overshoot into a false negative).
evidence: 7/7 with neg=ok subpath=y. Confirms A3 and B3 hold on real repos, not just fixtures - previously the suite could not distinguish a correct rule from one that flags everything.

title: Assert performance envelopes in the harness
note: max_onboard_seconds = 3x baseline with a 30s floor, soft-asserted so upstream repo growth does not cause flakes. Counts stay volatile.

note: --repo-path with --data-module/--data-symbol/--route-dir/--clean-module/--declare. Prints one result row, never compares to or writes the baseline. Verified against the A6 Supabase fixture: PASS.

Real dynamic dispatch matches none, so the gap is NOT detected and line-ordering dominance proceeds as if flow were straight-line. The safety valve only opens for test inputs.

title: An inference heuristic hardcodes dub auth helper name, and it is load-bearing

That result exists because dub is one of the eval repos and its helper name is compiled into the engine. It is not evidence inference generalises. T26 will correctly remove it and cost that candidate.

title: Verify B5 typed-error claim
note: Premise CONFIRMED: 8 sites, 7 in run-cli.ts plus one in rust-engine.ts. All are user-facing classification, not internal.
evidence: run-cli.ts:101,148 (Scan is stale), 160,161 (No repo contract), 174 (DRIFT_ENGINE_BIN/Rust engine), 185 (unsupported schema), 196 (Missing --db); rust-engine.ts:205.

The remaining two are check_command.rs:655-665 silent continue on unreadable files and :1865 zero security findings when repo_root is absent. title: Audit for other unconditional capability assertions
note: 22 sites classified in docs/architecture/capability-assertion-audit.md. One real overclaim fixed: candidate inference reported complete:true unconditionally while deciding the data layer by five-substring match - on midday it finds nothing and claimed full coverage. Standing rule recorded: any new complete/can_block/verified/proven field must be computed or carry a comment justifying the constant.

title: Disk exhaustion produced two false test failures mid-run
evidence: Free space hit 1.8GB. pnpm -r test reported 2 failures (doctor state, version metadata) and the external suite reported "database or disk is full" for formbricks and calcom. All passed on retry after remediation with no code change.
diagnosis: Confirms halt condition #1 is correctly placed - low disk yields untrustworthy results, not merely slow ones. Remediation: removed ~/.drift, tmp fixtures, and three unused clones (supabasestudio 1.3G, basejump, documenso). Note for future runs: cargo clean --release deletes the engine binary the harness needs; rebuild after. Reinforces T40/T41 priority.

title: Run halted cleanly: context exhausted after Phase 1 and Phase 2
needs: Resume at T12 per docs/autonomous-run/HALT.md. Tree green, nothing pushed, 7/7 suite passing.

title: Invert the factgraph fail-open completeness default and wire the engine measurement through
note: Both factgraph completeness fallbacks now default to complete:false with missing_capabilities [completeness_not_reported] and a reason, instead of claiming full coverage plus blocking authority when a caller omits the measurement.
evidence: Flipping the default made three existing tests fail, which turned out to be the real finding: the storage test, the query test AND the CLI prepare test all relied on the optimistic default, meaning ScanData never carried the engine completeness at all. A4 computed complete:false honestly and the factgraph then overwrote it with a constant, so the fix was invisible to users. completeness is now threaded from the scan_completed stream event (which already carried it) through ScanData into both constructors. Verified end-to-end: a repo with a non-UTF-8 file now reports complete:false with reason "1 file(s) could not be read or parsed and were skipped" via drift scan status.
diagnosis: Tests that asserted the optimistic default were changed to declare completeness explicitly rather than having their assertions flipped, so both paths stay documented.

title: Symbol-level type classification: drop imports used only in type positions
note: dub baseline findings 458 -> 417; type-only false-positive rate 8.5% -> 3.1%, with real headroom under the <10% gate. Zero reconciliation gaps.
evidence: Implemented on the AST, not by matching text: tree-sitter-typescript parses a name used as a type as type_identifier and as a value as identifier, so the distinction is the grammar own. Conservative by design - a binding is dropped only on positive evidence (at least one type use, no value use), because wrongly dropping a real data client would be a silent miss, the worst failure class here. Prisma (used for instanceof error classes AND as a type) is correctly kept.
diagnosis: Also forced the structural fix the plan wanted in B3: the Rust change immediately recreated the TS/Rust parser divergence A3 had closed, and A3.3 caught it as 3 reconciliation gaps rather than a crash. runFullRepoCheck now reads engine import facts directly instead of re-deriving them with the CLI regex, so there is one parser and the divergence class is gone permanently.

title: Verified against a stale release binary after a Rust source fix
evidence: Corrected the T12 retain predicate, ran cargo test (debug) which passed, then measured against target/release which still held the inverted logic - producing a misleading 8.4% result and 3 spurious reconciliation gaps. Rebuilding release gave the true 3.1%.
diagnosis: PROTOCOL.md already records "pnpm build after every source edit"; it needs the same for cargo build --release, since cargo test does not refresh the release binary the harness and CLI use. Amending.

title: Reduce whitelist over-matching
note: cal.com forbidden_imports 6 -> 1: exactly ["@calcom/prisma"], its real data layer. openstatus 4 -> 3, keeping @openstatus/db/src/schema.
evidence: Two boundary fixes. (1) Data-layer names must occur at a path or word boundary, not mid-identifier - @calcom/lib/isPrismaObj matched "prisma" inside a camelCase identifier and was recorded as a database client. (2) The /client rule required the same, because videoClient.ts - a conferencing service that queries the DB - read as a database client; a route importing a service that owns its data access is delegating correctly, so flagging it inverted the convention. Also excluded type-surface subpaths /enums, /zod-utils, /types, /constants, comparing with the file extension stripped so both the specifier and resolved-file forms are covered.
diagnosis: /schema deliberately NOT excluded: in a Drizzle repo the schema module IS the data layer (@openstatus/db/src/schema is imported at runtime and passed to queries), so excluding it would trade false positives for a false negative on a real data layer. Verified openstatus keeps it.

title: Boundary rule drops ../../lib/prismaClient, a legitimate client specifier
evidence: cal.com previously listed ../../lib/prismaClient; the word-boundary rule drops it because "prisma" is followed by "C" and "client" is preceded by "prisma", so neither token sits at a boundary in the lowercased string.
diagnosis: Accepted for now: the primary and correct specifier @calcom/prisma is retained, and a camelCase-aware boundary cannot separate prismaClient (a real client) from isPrismaObj (a type guard) - both are camelCase word boundaries. Distinguishing them needs the structural signal (does the module export an instantiated client), which is E2 scope. Logged so the false negative is visible rather than silently accepted.

title: Assert exact forbidden_imports sets
note: expectForbiddenExact pins the full set for taxonomy, formbricks, calcom and openstatus; expectForbidden alone only proved the real data layer was present, so cal.com passed while carrying four wrong entries out of six. dub/papermark/midday left as null pending a decision on their expected exact sets.

title: Disk preflight in the external suite
note: The suite now refuses to start below 5GB free with exit 3 and the remediation command, rather than failing mid-run. Disk exhaustion happened twice this session; the first time it produced four false failures, the second left the tool unable to write output at all. The drift CLI itself still needs the same preflight (T41 proper).

title: Version-gate incremental scan reuse
note: Reuse was keyed only on content_hash and byte_size, which assumes a file always yields the same facts. T12 (stop emitting type-only imports) and T13 (narrow data-layer matching) both broke that assumption, so upgrading Drift and rescanning would have silently kept stale facts for every unchanged file - stale analysis presented as current, the exact failure this product exists to prevent.
evidence: Proven end-to-end with hand-written manifests carrying a planted STALE_FACT that reparsing cannot produce: matching version reuses it (reuse_applied true, fact present), 9.9.9-different reparses (fact absent), absent version reparses. Locked in as crates/drift-engine/tests/scan_reuse.rs covering all three.
diagnosis: Required threading the engine version end-to-end: the scan_started stream event already carried engine_version and the CLI simply ignored it, and the CLI persisted adapter_versions from its own constants rather than from the engine. Same shape as the completeness bug in T11b - the engine reported something true and the CLI dropped it. Also note DRIFT_SCANNER_VERSION and DRIFT_ENGINE_VERSION are separate constants that happen to both be 0.1.0, which is why a proxy could not be used; T63 (single-source the version) is the real fix.

title: Disk-space preflight in doctor and start
note: doctor gains a disk_space check reporting free space against an estimate scaled by indexable file count (~220KB of state per file, measured across the eval repos); start refuses with exit 3 and names the remedy rather than only the problem. The external suite already refuses below 5GB from the earlier partial.
evidence: Direct evidence from two exhaustion events this session: the first produced four false test failures that all passed on retry with no code change, the second left no space for tool output at all. 5 tests including the first-run case where the state directory does not exist yet.

title: Pin version-constant coupling
note: Four TypeScript constants plus the Rust DRIFT_ENGINE_VERSION all read 0.1.0 independently, which makes them look interchangeable. T15 proved they are not: incremental reuse needs the engine version and no TypeScript constant tracks it, so the version had to be threaded from the engine scan_started event. Tests now pin the coupling to package.json and Cargo.toml so a bump cannot silently desynchronise them. Genuinely single-sourcing (generate from one file) is still open.

title: Stop storing the fact graph twice
note: dub per-repo state 599 MB -> 394 MB, a 34% reduction, with no functional change.
evidence: Profiled with dbstat: fact_graph_artifacts.graph_json was 206 MB of a 599 MB database while graph_nodes/graph_edges/graph_evidence held the same data relationally in 201 MB. The write path already normalized all of it, then serialized a second full copy. Enumerated every read of the blob first - only .graph.completeness (3 sites) and .graph.adapters (1) are ever accessed, and nodes/edges/evidence are only ever read via the normalized tables. graph_json now stores the small metadata only, and getFactGraphArtifact rehydrates the collections from those tables so the artifact callers receive is identical.
diagnosis: Remaining top consumers are the legitimate normalized tables (graph_edges 100MB, graph_evidence 51MB, graph_nodes 50MB, facts 36MB). Further reduction means either scan retention (keep N most recent) or narrowing what the graph records - a bigger design question than deduplication, so left open.

title: Concurrency: busy_timeout for hook + CLI + MCP
note: WAL and foreign_keys were already on but busy_timeout was absent, so two concurrent writers hit SQLITE_BUSY immediately - reaching the user as a crash rather than a brief wait. Set to 5000ms, which comfortably covers a single-file check. Three tests: pragmas set, a second connection reads while the first holds the database, and 20 interleaved writes from two connections all land.
diagnosis: Unblocks T44 (hooks pack), whose whole premise is an edit-time check running while the developer and possibly an agent also hold the database.

title: Deleted-file handling in check
note: Verified on formbricks: deleting the baselined violating route yields 0 findings, the path is recorded in skipped_deleted_files, deleted_file_count is 1, and no orphaned or re-reported finding appears. Behaviour was already correct; now pinned by tests.

title: Renamed/moved route handling
note: The concern did NOT materialise. I expected a git rename to present as delete+add, which under A5 block-new would punish a refactor by treating a moved legacy violation as new code.
evidence: Verified on formbricks with its single baselined violation. Pure rename: no findings, status pass. Rename + unrelated edit: the violation is found at the new path with enforcement_result=block but diff_status=touched_existing, so blocking_count stays 0 - correct, because the violating line is not a changed line. A new violation written into a changed line of a moved file still blocks.
diagnosis: Correct for a fragile reason: it depends on git reporting renames as renames and on the diff parser, not on an explicit rename rule. Five tests now pin added/renamed/deleted classification so this cannot silently regress.

title: Define the FP metric in the DoD
note: Definition fixed in PLAN.md: type-only usage counts as a false positive; a runtime import of the data package that is not itself a query (the Prisma error-namespace case) does not, and is documented as policy. Enforcement is the T03 per-repo negative control, not a rate threshold, because after T12 the engine cannot emit a type-only finding by construction.
evidence: Built the rate calculation first and it was wrong: it put cal.com at 12.8% and failed the gate, but all five "false positives" were `import { prisma } from "@calcom/prisma"` - genuine client imports - misclassified because the regex looks for prisma followed by . or ( and the real usage was `new CalendarCacheEventRepository(prisma)`, passing it as an argument.
diagnosis: The classifier was strictly weaker than the engine AST detection it was meant to audit, so it could only add noise to a property the engine already guarantees. Removed rather than shipped. Recorded in the plan as a rejected approach because it looked correct.

title: Docs audit against A5 behaviour changes
diagnosis: Expected docs describing exit 1 for a blocked check to be wrong after A5. They were not: the README and docs never documented drift check exit codes at all, and the only exit-1 references are about the CI gate script. Nothing became stale. The real gap is the inverse - exit codes are now a documented contract with nothing documenting them - which is T73, done alongside.

title: Document the enforcement model honestly
note: docs/reference/enforcement.md explains why the same violation blocks on formbricks/cal.com/openstatus and only warns on taxonomy/dub/papermark, with the real ratios. Without that explanation the split reads as inconsistency; it is the coverage-direction gate refusing to reject code written like its neighbours.

title: Exit-code and JSON contract reference
note: Exit codes now in drift --help and in docs/reference/enforcement.md, plus the three fields that get conflated: check.status (did anything blocking happen), finding.enforcement_result (what would this convention do), summary.blocking_count (how many actually block). Documents that enforcement_result block with status pass is not a contradiction, the diff-status semantics including added/renamed/deleted files, the baseline, and how to read completeness.

title: Gitignore correctness via the ignore crate
attempted: Replaced the hand-rolled IgnoreMatcher with ignore::gitignore::GitignoreBuilder rooted at the repo, adding every .gitignore discovered in the tree. Fixture verification passed: nested .gitignore honored (was not) and ! negations honored (were discarded).
evidence: The external suite caught a real regression on openstatus - injection_caught true -> false, catches_genuine_subpath true -> false, status PASS -> FAIL. Root cause: apps/server/.gitignore contains a bare pattern `app`, and GitignoreBuilder::add() interprets patterns relative to the *builder root*, not the added file directory. So a pattern scoped to apps/server/ went repo-wide and excluded apps/dashboard/src/app/ - swallowing openstatus real API routes.
diagnosis: My approach was wrong, not the crate. Per-directory scoping is normally handled by ignore::WalkBuilder, which constructs a separate Gitignore per directory and applies precedence nearest-first. Reverted: a wrong ignore implementation that silently excludes real routes is far worse than the original limitation, since excluded files produce no findings at all.
needs: Either (a) build one Gitignore per directory rooted at that directory and test a path against each applicable one nearest-first, or (b) adopt ignore::WalkBuilder for file discovery, which handles this natively but replaces the existing walk. (b) is cleaner but larger. Note the fixture from T08 passes under the naive approach, so fixture-only verification is insufficient here - the suite is what caught it.

title: Storage migration path for existing users
note: Forward migration verified: id-based, forward-only, idempotent, and a database that stopped at migration 8 upgrades to all 27 with data intact. Ids are asserted unique, since they are the upgrade key and a duplicate or rename would silently skip a migration on an existing install.
evidence: The gap was the reverse direction and it was unguarded: an older build opening a database written by a newer Drift saw only migration ids it did not recognise, found all of its own already applied, applied nothing, and then operated against a schema containing tables and columns it knew nothing about - a silent wrong answer rather than a failure. Now refused with a message naming the remedy, using the wording run-cli.ts already classifies as a refusal.
diagnosis: 4 tests. Note the legacy-write case had to use raw SQL: upsertRepo sets columns added by later migrations, which is precisely what an older build could not have done, so using the modern writer would not have tested anything real.

title: Baseline drift semantics when a baselined file changes
attempted: Mapped the full four-case matrix on formbricks, then changed the blocking predicates (blockingCount, blockingNewHunks, warnings, preExisting accounting) so a finding blocks on diff_status=new_in_diff + block regardless of baseline status. Verified all four cases behaved as the plan pre-registered. Reverted after two existing tests failed.
evidence: Matrix as shipped: (1) untouched baselined violation -> no finding, pass. (2) file edited elsewhere -> pre_existing/touched_existing, pass. (3) violating line itself REWRITTEN -> pre_existing/new_in_diff/block but blocking_count 0, pass. (4) violation REMOVED, committed, then REINTRODUCED -> same, pass. So a baseline fingerprint match is a permanent per-violation waiver: rewriting the line or deleting and re-adding it stays exempt forever. My plan pre-registered that (4) must block.
diagnosis: Not a bug - a product decision, and two tests encode the current contract explicitly ("does not fail check for active baseline findings" reuses the same diff that otherwise exits 2, and "preserves human-governed finding statuses during repeated checks"). The tension is that --accept-defaults baselines everything automatically, so an onboarding-time bulk shield is being treated as a considered per-finding waiver. baseline_violations has no provenance column, so the two cannot be distinguished today.
needs: A decision between: (A) keep as-is, baseline = permanent per-fingerprint waiver; (B) baseline shields untouched code only, so rewriting or reintroducing a violation blocks - stronger promise, breaks the tested contract, makes previously-passing diffs fail; (C) add a provenance column to baseline_violations and honour explicit waivers permanently while onboarding baselines shield only untouched code. Recommend C: Drift already has explicit waiver mechanisms (findings suppress, contract waivers), so the bulk onboarding baseline should not silently double as one. C needs a migration, hence the decision.

title: Contract portability across machines
diagnosis: The stated concern - that importing a contract from an unrelated repo would be silently accepted - is false. Importing cal.com contract into taxonomy returns imported:false, compatible:false, with reasons [repo_id_mismatch, repo_fingerprint_mismatch]. My first probe reported ACCEPTED only because it checked for an error key rather than reading the compatibility block. The safety check works.
evidence: Verified both directions on real repos with separate temp HOMEs.

title: Contract portability is impossible, which invalidates E3 drift.lock premise
attempted: Exported taxonomy contract on one checkout and imported it into a second checkout of the same repo at a different path.
evidence: Refused: imported:false, reasons [repo_id_mismatch, repo_fingerprint_mismatch]. Root cause is repoIdForRoot in packages/cli/src/domain/identifiers.ts - repo_${hashStable(resolve(repoRoot))} - so repo identity is derived from the ABSOLUTE PATH. Every teammate checkout is a different repo as far as Drift is concerned, and the repo_fingerprint carries the same derivation.
diagnosis: The compatibility check is correct for foreign contracts; the problem is that path-derived identity cannot distinguish "same repo, different checkout" from "different repo". Direct consequence: E3 pitches contract export as a committed, PR-reviewable drift.lock - a package-lock for your conventions - and that cannot work today, because no teammate can import the committed contract. E4 (GitHub Action) has the same problem: CI checks out to a different path than any developer.
needs: A path-independent repo identity before E3 or E4 can ship. Options: (a) derive from git remote URL plus root commit sha - stable across clones, breaks for repos with no remote; (b) derive from repo content (e.g. root package.json name plus root commit) - no remote needed; (c) allow import with an explicit --allow-path-mismatch flag, cheapest but leaves the identity wrong everywhere else. Recommend (a) with (b) as fallback. This is a design decision affecting stored ids, so it needs a migration story too.

title: Typed errors for user-facing failures
note: Added DriftError carrying its own failure code, user action, recovery commands and retryability. The top-level classifier now reads error.code first and falls back to the existing string matching, so this is incremental rather than a rewrite and no throw site breaks. Migrated the two highest-value sites: missing_contract in repo-paths.ts and insufficient_disk in start.ts (which also converts the disk refusal from a hand-built exit-3 payload into a classified throw).
evidence: T09 found 8 message-matching sites, all user-facing. The stale-scan branch maps to exit 3 after A5, so rewording an error string silently changed exit-code behaviour. 4 tests, including that rewording a message does not change its classification.
diagnosis: Remaining string-matched branches are stale_scan, missing_engine, unsupported_database and missing_database. Note storage cannot import from the CLI package, so the T16 migration guard keeps its wording contract; making that typed needs a shared error module or a code carried on the storage error, which is a small design choice rather than a mechanical migration.

title: Error-message quality pass
note: Added the three codes that previously reached users as raw SQLite or filesystem strings: disk_full (I hit "database or disk is full" verbatim mid-scan, with no indication of what to do), corrupt_database and permission_denied. Each carries a cause, a next action, recovery commands, and an honest safe_to_retry - false for corrupt_database and permission_denied, since rerunning cannot fix either and inviting a retry loop wastes time.
evidence: docs/reference/errors.md tables all ten codes with cause, whether retrying helps, and the remedy, plus how to add one. 3 tests assert that no reported failure ever lacks a code, an action, or a recovery command - a catch-all is acceptable, a catch-all that says nothing useful is not.
diagnosis: Also documents that four codes are refusals rather than errors and map to exit 3, so a caller can distinguish "no enforcement claim was made" from "the diff violates the contract" and from "drift broke".

title: Verify secret redaction actually applies
note: Canary test across six surfaces (prepare, ask, repo map, contract show, scan status, findings list) with a marked secret in .env, apps/web/.env and server.pem: zero leaks. Then pinned the mechanism with 15 policy tests.
evidence: Important nuance the canary test alone would have hidden: the secret files were never indexed, because Drift only indexes TS/JS. That protection is incidental, not the policy. The actual mechanism is the deny-glob filter in preflight.ts, applied in two places - the indexable-file walk AND an explicitly requested targetPath - and confirmed present in both.
diagnosis: That deny-glob filter is exactly what F9 broke: the old glob compiler made **/*.pem require a leading slash, so a root-level server.pem was not denied. The new tests assert the precise shapes that bug let through (root-level pem, nested apps/web/.env), plus repo-escape refusal and the full-file-content switch, so a glob regression can never silently reopen it.

title: Pin CLI-side enforcement of engine-ignored contract fields
note: Rewritten from B2, whose premise was false. The engine does bind waivers/exceptions/scope/governance to _ in check_command.rs, but the CLI applies them at every enforcement site, so it is layering rather than a fail-open - and implementing B2 as written would have broken every contract using an exception or waiver.
evidence: 6 tests, one per field the engine drops, covering the cases that matter: an exception stops applying once it expires rather than becoming a permanent hole; an import-level exception is scoped to the named symbol and source rather than the whole file; a waiver expires; and a waiver requiring reapproval stops applying when the content hash changes and is not kept alive by a different file in the same waiver.
diagnosis: The real risk was never a fail-open, it was that the layering is undocumented and unpinned - nothing stopped someone deleting the CLI-side checks on the reasonable grounds that the engine should own enforcement, at which point contracts would silently stop being honoured while every check still reported success. docs/concepts/enforcement-layers.md records the split and the rule: if the engine ignores a field, the CLI must enforce it AND a test must prove it. Also caught my own misreading - approval is recorded per file via approved_file_hashes, not a single hash.

title: Map every contract field to its enforcement site
note: Mapped all RepoContract fields. 13 are genuinely enforced. SEVEN are declared in the schema and read by nothing: enforcement_policy, active_convention_rule_ids, beta_claim_profile, active_semantic_capability_ids, architecture_contract_id, architecture_contract_fingerprint, semantic_capability_contract_version. layer_architecture is a near-miss - written by contract-materialization but never read back.
evidence: Three of the seven (enforcement_policy, beta_claim_profile, active_semantic_capability_ids) were found by the tripwire test rather than by reading the interface - I had enumerated four by hand and missed them. enforcement_policy is the most misleading: the name reads as the control for how enforcement behaves, and writing it does nothing.
diagnosis: Same shape as F3 and A4 - a confident-looking declaration with nothing behind it - except the declaration is the operator own, which makes the silence harder to notice because they wrote it and got no complaint. NOT rejecting them at import yet: each needs a call the schema cannot make (implement, remove, or mark experimental), and rejecting a field that may already be in committed contracts is breaking. Recorded with a recommendation per field, plus a tripwire test so the list cannot grow unnoticed.

title: Gate the security heuristics layer behind --experimental-security
note: Security convention kinds are hidden from listings by default and can never be auto-accepted by --accept-defaults. On dub the default listing drops from 20 candidates to 1 (the layering wedge), with 19 security candidates hidden AND reported, plus the reveal command. Verified the accepted default convention is still the data-access one.
evidence: Scoped strictly from T07 rather than assumed: all five audit claims were confirmed there, the sharpest being that unsupported_dynamic_control_flow() - the valve meant to degrade a proof when control flow is too dynamic - matches only Drift fixture strings, so it opens for test inputs and never for real dynamic dispatch. Auto-accept mattered because on several real repos an auth-helper candidate ranks first, so onboarding would silently have enabled the layer.
diagnosis: Also reworded the two user-facing reason strings away from proof/dominance vocabulary ("Unsupported dynamic control flow prevents auth dominance proof" -> "Dynamic control flow could not be analysed, so auth coverage for this route is unknown"), and blocked security_boundary_proofs and auth_dominance_analysis as claims in both capabilities.ts and beta-claims.json with the lift condition. The 12 hardcoded can_block:true sites in security_capabilities.rs stay as-is deliberately: the layer is now gated, so fixing them individually would be wasted work ahead of the AST rebuild.

title: Remove test-tailored literals from production paths
note: Removed "withworkspace" from the auth-helper name list, and generalised the dynamic-control-flow valve from three fixture strings to actual dispatch shapes.
evidence: The withworkspace removal cost a candidate and inverted a test, which is the point. That test was named infer_candidates_learns_workspace_wrappers_as_auth_patterns and asserted Drift LEARNS such wrappers - it passed only because dub auth wrapper name was compiled into the engine, and dub is an evaluation repo. Renamed to does_not_recognise_repo_specific_wrappers_as_auth_helpers with the assertion inverted, recording the honest baseline. This directly revises the falsification report claim that withWorkspace at 253 occurrences was the most useful output across six repos.
diagnosis: The valve fix mattered more than expected. My first generalisation scanned line by line and broke a security test, because the real fixture shape splits the lookup and the call across two lines - const guard = guards[...] then await guard(). That is also the common shape in real code, so a line-at-a-time scan would have been another check that only appears to work. It now correlates a binding assigned from a collection lookup with a later invocation of that binding. Left: driftSensitive and parseRequestBody( in security_facts.rs. Neither appears in any fixture or doc, so they only fire on code that happens to use those exact identifiers, but removing them deletes the capability rather than fixing it - it needs a documented annotation or a real detection strategy, which is AST-rebuild scope and the layer is now gated behind --experimental-security anyway.

title: Claims to behaviour reconciliation
note: Every allowed claim is now mapped to the test that proves it, and adding an allowed claim without evidence fails the suite. Also asserts the JSON manifest stays in step with the code manifest, and that the four demoted claims (convention_learning, automatic_convention_inference_for_any_data_layer, security_boundary_proofs, auth_dominance_analysis) stay blocked - a regression re-allowing them would be an overclaim, not a feature.
evidence: 10 tests. accepted_contract_blocks_direct_data_access is backed by the seven-repo baseline rather than a unit test, since injection caught with correct evidence on every real repo is the actual proof. incremental_reuse is backed by the T15 version-gate test.
diagnosis: A hand-maintained claims file drifts from behaviour silently, which is the exact failure this product exists to prevent - a poor thing to ship.

title: Large-repo scaling probe
note: Measured envelope on a synthetic 20k-file repo (4k routes) documented in docs/reference/performance.md. Onboarding 19.5s, check on one changed file 2.4s, state 226MB - all fine. prepare 27.7s and repo map ~100s are not.
evidence: Issue #99 REPRODUCED. CPU profiling attributed prepare 31s to listGraphNodes/listGraphEdges/listGraphEvidence called several times each, plus ~5s GC. Root cause of part of it was my own T40 change: getFactGraphArtifact hydrated the bulk collections eagerly, so every call ran three full table scans. Made it lazy and memoized - ask 2.2s->0.7s, scan status 2.1s->0.6s.
diagnosis: prepare and repo map still traverse the whole graph because they genuinely use it; that needs scoped loading or indexed queries, not a micro-fix. prepare is the surface the context claim rests on and the one T44 hooks pack calls at edit time, so fixing it is a prerequisite for that pack rather than a follow-up. Also recorded a wrong guess honestly: I first blamed RegExp compilation and memoized it, which changed nothing - the comment now says so rather than claiming a measurement I did not make.

title: Memory ceiling under load
note: Measured peak RSS on 20k files: Rust engine 93MB, Node CLI 1.76GB - 19x, for the same scan. The CLI holds the whole payload (86k facts plus graph nodes/edges/evidence) as JS objects. Heap ceiling found by capping max-old-space-size: 512MB crashes, 1024MB works. Working rule documented: ~52KB heap per indexable file.
evidence: The 512MB crash was uncontrolled - FATAL ERROR: JavaScript heap out of memory, exit 134, no Drift error, no failure code, no next action, and a partially written database. Constrained CI runners cap Node heap routinely, so this is a real configuration. Now doctor reports a memory_headroom check and start refuses up front with the exact NODE_OPTIONS line, verified end to end: the same 512MB invocation that crashed now returns a classified insufficient_memory refusal.
diagnosis: No OOM at the sizes Drift targets provided the heap is adequate, but the 19x gap is the real story - a 60k-file monorepo would need ~3GB and should be treated as unsupported until the CLI streams into storage rather than buffering the whole payload. That is the same underlying shape as T42: the CLI materialises the entire graph where it should work incrementally.

title: Incremental single-file check performance
note: formbricks single-file check 6.9s -> 3.9s (43%). Root cause: drift check called collectScanData with NO reuse manifest, so every check re-parsed the entire repository through the engine even for a one-line edit. Profiling showed 5.1s of the 6.9s was the Node process sitting idle waiting on the engine subprocess.
evidence: The reuse machinery already existed and collectScanData already accepted reuseManifestPath - only scan passed one, check never did. Safe to enable because of T15 version gate: facts from a different engine are refused, so reuse cannot serve stale extraction after an upgrade. Confirmed working by comparison: the engine full scan alone takes 5.39s on formbricks, and check now completes in 3.9s.
diagnosis: Remaining 3.9s is the engine still walking and hashing all ~4000 files to decide what is reusable, plus CLI graph assembly. Reaching the sub-1s target needs a changed-files-only engine mode that skips hashing unchanged files entirely - a real feature, not a wiring fix. Also noted: the check payload does not surface reuse stats (files_reused/reuse_applied are absent), so this improvement is invisible to users and untestable by assertion; worth adding.

title: Hooks pack (E1, the launch headline)
attempted: Measured the edit-time path before writing the hook, since the DoD requires blocking in under 1s.
evidence: On formbricks a single-file check took 6.9s before T45 and 3.9s after - still ~4x the DoD. Detection itself is correct: exit 2 with blocking_count 1 for a violating edit, exit 0 for a clean edit, verified on the warn/block split.
diagnosis: Deliberately not shipping the hook at this latency. E1 is the item that makes Drift agent-native rather than another linter, and a 4-second pause on every file edit would undermine exactly that claim - a slow guardrail gets disabled, and a disabled guardrail enforces nothing. The correctness half is proven and ready; only the speed is missing.
needs: T45 completed to its sub-1s target via a changed-files-only engine mode. Once check is under 1s the hook itself is a small piece of work, and the block/warn messaging is already specified in docs/reference/enforcement.md.

title: drift prepare quality eval (the context claim)
note: Found prepare essentially broken for its stated purpose, fixed it, and added a measuring harness. pnpm eval:prepare - 3/3 tasks now surface the expected file at rank 4, 1, 1.
evidence: On dub, "add an endpoint that lists workspace invites" returned 25 files of which 24 were arbitrary API routes matched only by "in scope for this convention" - true of every route in the repo. ZERO matched "invite", despite dub having five invite routes including apps/web/app/api/workspaces/[idOrSlug]/invites/route.ts, the one file that task is about. Root cause: files.slice(0,25) applied in filesystem-walk order, so the cap was exhausted on app/(ee)/api/admin/* before the walk reached the relevant directory. There was no ranking at all. Added relevance scoring - task-token matches dominate convention scope, since scope only says a file is the kind of thing the rule applies to. dub now returns 24 relevant of 25 with the target at rank 4.
diagnosis: This is the differentiated claim - query established patterns rather than audit for them - and it shipped with no test of output quality, only that something was returned. Kept out of external-eval.mjs because prepare takes ~50s on dub and would triple the runtime of the suite that gates every change; that slowness is T42/T45 work. Note the original DoD asked to assert withWorkspace surfaces, which T26 deliberately removed - the harness asserts task-relevant files instead, which is the durable property.

title: MCP protocol revision risk assessment
note: Verdict: GO for beta, not launch-blocking. docs/architecture/mcp-compatibility.md records the finding with evidence.
evidence: Probed the real entry point (packages/mcp/dist/bin.js - note index.js is a library with no main, which cost me two failed probe rounds) with four client-declared versions: 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2026-07-28. The server accepts ALL of them without error and replies with its own 2024-11-05, which is the spec-correct posture. A full session then completes against a client declaring 2025-06-18: initialize ok, tools/list 12 tools, tools/call returns content. So the failure mode is not the server turning clients away; it is a client refusing an old revision, which is client-side policy.
diagnosis: Two of the three cited breaking changes (Mcp-Session-Id removal, SSE to InputRequiredResult) are HTTP transport concerns and this server is stdio-only, so they do not apply. IMPORTANT LIMIT stated in the doc: I could not verify the 2026-07-28 revision exists or what it contains - my knowledge cutoff predates it and I had no network evidence. The measured behaviour stands regardless, but that specific claim is unverified and should be re-checked against the published spec. DoD asked for two real clients; I tested one scripted spec-following stdio client, so this is PARTIAL. 4 tests pin the negotiation posture, including that the server must NOT echo the client version - the tempting fix, which would silently claim semantics it may not implement.

title: Trim the MCP preflight packet
note: Measured the packet for the first time: 84,729 bytes / ~21,000 tokens for ONE get_task_preflight call on taxonomy - a 131-file repo. 33 top-level keys. Removed legacy_packet (3,012 bytes), taking it to 80,012 / ~20,000 tokens. DoD of <=12 top-level keys NOT met.
evidence: Field-by-field measurement: graph_context 20,378; task_preflight_packet 14,861 (of which parser_gaps 6,287 and legacy_packet 3,012); scan_status 7,376. Three-layer nesting - top level -> task_preflight_packet -> legacy_packet - with seven fields inside task_preflight_packet byte-identical to top-level siblings (4,008 bytes) and legacy_packet byte-identical to the top-level agent_contract_packet. Removed the latter: it is named legacy, duplicates a sibling exactly, and the schema now marks it optional so a consumer still reading it parses rather than throws. Test asserts it is absent rather than merely unasserted.
diagnosis: Did NOT do the 33->12 structural collapse. It changes every field path for every MCP consumer, so it needs a response_schema version bump and a migration note - a deliberate decision, not something to land unattended late in a run. The remaining bulk is real content, not duplication: graph_context alone is 24% of the packet and is the same whole-graph materialisation behind T42 repo map 100s, so scoped graph loading would shrink this too. Recommend doing the collapse and the T42 scoped loading together behind one schema bump.

title: drift.lock framing (E3)
needs: T19b — a path-independent repo identity. E3 pitches contract export as a committed, PR-reviewable drift.lock, and T19b proved no teammate can import one: repoIdForRoot hashes the ABSOLUTE PATH, so every checkout is a different repo and contract import refuses with repo_id_mismatch and repo_fingerprint_mismatch. Framing the feature before it can work would document something users cannot do.

title: GitHub Action (E4)
needs: T19b, same root cause. CI checks out to a path no developer shares, so the Action cannot consume a committed contract either. Also gated behind T45: a check that takes 3.9s on formbricks is tolerable in CI, unlike at edit time, so this is less severe here than for T44 — but the identity problem is fatal.

title: MCP SDK migration
needs: Explicitly gated in the plan as not before 2026-07-28, and T47 found no reason to bring it forward: the current hand-rolled server negotiates correctly, accepts clients two revisions newer, and serves a full session. Note T47 could not verify what the 2026-07-28 revision actually contains, so the trigger for this task is itself unconfirmed.

title: CLI/MCP payload deduplication (C4)
note: Extracted relevance ranking into @drift/query and pointed both surfaces at it. This was not cleanup - it fixed a live bug I had just caused.
evidence: T46 added relevance ranking to packages/cli/src/domain/preflight.ts. MCP has its own copy of that whole assembly (13 duplicated functions in preflight alone, plus ~12 more mirroring CLI domain helpers), so get_task_preflight - the surface agents actually call - kept returning filesystem-order results. Verified against the live MCP server on dub: 0 of 25 files matched invite, and the top hits were arbitrary admin routes. After the fix: 8 of 25, with the four invites routes on top, identical to the CLI. Same divergence class as the TypeScript/Rust import bug B3 and T12 closed.
diagnosis: MCP also truncated to 25 DURING the walk, before any ranking could run, so simply sharing the ranking function was not enough - the cap had already discarded the files that should have won. Removed. Remaining duplication (~25 functions) is not yet extracted; the parity tests were NOT deleted as the DoD suggested, because check-parity.test.ts polices engine-vs-TypeScript parity, which T12 depends on, rather than the CLI/MCP duplication this task targets.

title: pnpm check:boundaries has been failing since before this run
evidence: packages/cli/src/domain/data-layer-discovery.ts uses raw SQLite; the check reports database access belongs in packages/storage. Confirmed pre-existing by stashing all my changes and re-running - still fails. git log -S traces it to 201f462 (the A6 work), and it is present at this run base commit 393f2ee.
diagnosis: A dependency-boundary gate that has been red since before the run is a gate nobody is reading, which is T53 subject. Worth noting the shape: the same class of thing this product exists to catch - a rule that is declared, checked, and ignored.

title: Enforce the CLI/MCP dependency boundary
note: Fixed the boundary gate itself, then added the CLI/MCP assertion the task asked for. pnpm check:boundaries is green for the first time since before this run.
evidence: The gate had been red since commit 201f462 (pre-run) on a FALSE POSITIVE: it tested source.includes("better-sqlite3"), which fired on data-layer-discovery.ts where that string is one entry in a list of known data-layer package names used for detection - not a database call. Now matches an actual import or require of the driver. Verified both directions: injecting a real `import Database from "better-sqlite3"` into repo-paths.ts is caught, and removing it goes green.
diagnosis: Then added the assertion the task is actually about - MCP must not import from the CLI - verified with a negative control (an injected @drift/cli import is caught). The boundary already held; this keeps a convenient import from quietly establishing the dependency, which matters more after T51 showed the two surfaces silently diverging. Worth naming the shape: a declared rule that was checked and ignored for months because it cried wolf, which is exactly what this product exists to catch.

title: Convert remaining repros to fixtures (C2)
note: Added two permanent fixtures with tests, covering the two falsification findings that guard work from this run: test/fixtures/type-only-imports (T12) and test/fixtures/binary-and-unreadable (A4). Rust suites 23 -> 24.
evidence: The type-only fixture covers both erasure forms in one route - a separate `import type` AND an inline `{ type Prisma, prisma }` modifier - alongside a genuine value use, so it asserts the distinction rather than just the absence. That distinction is what took dub 8.5% -> 3.1%. The binary fixture holds a .ts file whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 plus a .png, asserting the scan completes, the readable route is still found, and the png is never indexed.
diagnosis: PARTIAL: three of the five artifacts T60 names are still unaddressed - root-layout injection e2e, entrypoint-dup, and the naming experiment as a parametrised eval. The naming experiment is largely subsumed by midday (T01), which is a real repo defeating the whitelist rather than a synthetic variant, so it is the least valuable of the three. Note 53 fixtures already existed; none of the five named ones did.

title: Lint, formatting, and the e2e gate
note: cargo fmt and clippy were both failing; both now green. The clippy error was mine from T12 - !(used_as_type && !used_as_value). Clippy suggested !used_as_type || used_as_value, which is the same predicate with the reasoning removed, so I named the concept instead: let erased_at_runtime = used_as_type && !used_as_value.
evidence: Also caught a real gap in my own discipline: I had been verifying with pnpm -r test (unit) plus the external suite, and never ran pnpm test:e2e, which verify:ci includes. It had 8 failures. Built the run base 393f2ee in a worktree and ran e2e there to attribute honestly: 6 of the 8 were already failing before this run. Two were mine and are fixed - the release-gate string assertion (I added pnpm test:harness to verify:ci in T04) and the golden snapshot (my new disk_space and memory_headroom doctor checks).
diagnosis: verify:ci already chains format:engine:check, lint:engine and check:boundaries - the gate existed, it was just red and unread, same as T53a. Now green except the 6 pre-existing e2e failures logged as T62a.

title: Six e2e tests have been failing since before this run
evidence: Attributed by building base commit 393f2ee in a worktree and running pnpm test:e2e there: release-hygiene beta proof, the dogfood MCP package-boundary enforcement proof, and four security fixture matrices (validation, tenant authorization, sensitive response, Phase 6) all fail at base. The security-validation one expects exit 1 where check now returns 2, which is A5 behaviour that predates this run.
diagnosis: Same shape as T53a: the release gate that would have caught these is verify:ci, and it has been red long enough that nobody runs it. Notably the four security matrices sit in the layer T25 just gated behind --experimental-security, so some may be obsoleted rather than fixed. The exit-1 expectation is the thing T70 went looking for and I concluded was absent - it was in the e2e tests, not the docs, which is why reading docs alone missed it.

title: Fix the six pre-existing e2e failures; verify:ci green
note: pnpm verify:ci now exits 0 - the full release gate (build, typecheck, unit, e2e, harness, rustfmt, clippy, boundaries, release matrix, claims, beta proof, git diff --check) passes for the first time since before this run. e2e 63/63.
evidence: Root cause of five of the six was one thing: A5 made a blocked check exit 2, and the e2e matrices plus run-beta-proof.mjs still expected 1. Nineteen stale expectations across four security matrices, the dogfood enforcement proof, and the beta proof exitCodes allowlist. Changed only where the case genuinely blocks - guarded on blockingCount>0, proven:false, or proofStatus in (missing_proof, parser_gap) - so a passing case expecting 0 was never touched.
diagnosis: The sixth was my own T48 being half-done: I removed legacy_packet from the MCP packet but the CLI builds its own copy and still emitted it, so the CLI/MCP parity check failed. Third time this run the duplication has bitten. Also improved run-beta-proof.mjs diagnostics: on a parity mismatch it dumped two 20KB payloads, and now names the differing paths - which is how I found the legacy_packet difference in one run instead of hand-diffing.

title: Split cli.test.ts as files are touched
note: Extracted the contiguous positional-argument family into cli-positional-args.test.ts and lifted the shared seedDatabase helper into test/support/. cli.test.ts 15,846 -> 15,772 lines. Package test count identical before and after: 436 -> 436.
evidence: Deliberately did NOT bulk-split. The families in that file are scattered - the 114 "rejects..." tests run from line 612 to line 15779 - so moving one would mean 114 individual relocations, and a test dropped in transit looks exactly like a test that passes. The 436 -> 436 count is the check that makes any future extraction safe to attempt.
diagnosis: The structural blocker was seedDatabase: 71 call sites, defined inline, so every extraction had to duplicate it - and two copies of a test seed drift apart the same way two copies of production code do, which this run has now demonstrated three times. It now lives in test/support/seed-database.ts and takes the caller tempDirs array, so each file keeps its own cleanup. That is the piece that makes the remaining splits mechanical rather than risky.

title: Test-isolation hardening
note: Removed --workspace-concurrency=1 from pnpm test. Four consecutive default-concurrency runs green across 789 tests in nine packages, then verify:ci exit 0.
evidence: The contention C3 was hiding was SQLITE_BUSY. WAL was on so readers never blocked the writer, but busy_timeout was never set, so two concurrent writers failed instantly rather than waiting milliseconds. Serialising the workspace made that impossible, which is precisely why it appeared to work.
diagnosis: T17 set busy_timeout=5000 for an unrelated reason - a hook, the CLI and an MCP server can all hold the database at once in normal use, and SQLITE_BUSY was reaching users as a crash. Fixing it for users fixed the suite. Verified empirically with four runs rather than assuming the connection. docs/architecture/test-isolation.md records what the contention was and what to check before reaching for serialisation again, including that low disk produced four false failures during this project that all passed on retry.

title: Mutation-style check on the enforcement core
note: All five core behaviours deliberately broken; every mutation caught, no new tests needed. Table in docs/architecture/mutation-check.md.
evidence: M1 glob **/ requires a leading segment (the F9 bug) -> 23 core tests. M2 is_api_route_path always false -> 1 Rust suite + 14 external repo checks. M3 is_forbidden_import always false -> 1 Rust suite + 14 external checks. M4 diff_status never new_in_diff (A5 regression) -> 7 CLI tests. M5 blocking counts warn instead of block -> 16 CLI tests.
diagnosis: The sharpest result is that M2 and M3 are caught by ONE Rust unit suite but by FOURTEEN checks across the seven eval repos - the external suite, not the unit tests, is what actually guards enforcement. That matches this run: unit tests stayed green through both regressions the suite caught (T22 gitignore, T51 ranking divergence). Also recorded a method trap I hit: a mutation must compile to be valid. My first M2 renamed a function instead of changing its body, the build failed, and the test count came back zero - which reads exactly like nothing caught it.

title: Prune docs to four documents (D3)
note: docs/ went from 71 markdown files with four stale specs at top level to three user-facing documents (quickstart, concepts, agent-integration) plus reference/, architecture/, autonomous-run/ and archive/. All internal links verified to resolve.
evidence: The three new documents did not exist and are the user-facing gap: quickstart explains why a repo warns instead of blocks (the question most likely to read as a bug), concepts walks files -> facts -> contract -> baseline -> check and states the inference limits plainly, agent-integration covers MCP, hooks and CI. Each is grounded in what this run verified rather than in intent - including that hooks are NOT shipped and why, and that a committed contract cannot yet be imported by CI or a teammate.
diagnosis: One deliberate deviation from the DoD: it asked for four top-level documents including a single reference. I kept reference/ as three focused documents (enforcement, errors, performance) because one monolithic reference is worse to use, and errors.md and performance.md are already cited from elsewhere. Archived rather than deleted the four stale specs plus eleven sprint plans, with a README mapping each to what supersedes it, because findings in architecture/ cite them.

title: README rewrite (D5)
note: First screen now answers what, for whom, and limits. Opens with one sentence and a four-line install-to-check block, then a scope table that says what Drift does NOT do before anything else.
evidence: Includes the measured 7/7 external results and the 3.1% false-positive rate rather than adjectives, and explains the warn-vs-block split with the real ratios (formbricks 1 of 83 blocks, dub ~323 of 494 warns) because that is the behaviour most likely to be read as a bug. States the inference limitation plainly - data layers are recognised by specifier substring, so store/supabase repos must declare with --data-modules - and that security heuristics are experimental and not proofs. All links verified to resolve.
diagnosis: PARTIAL by design: the DoD also asks for a 60-second GIF (start -> inject -> blocked), which I cannot record, and says verification is human review and must not be self-approved. Flagging for review rather than marking done.
